The slide title is: Mastering MongoDB. You will also see the heading: Document modeling, queries, aggregation, and production operations. The slide says: Innovation In Software · 3 days · Introductory to intermediate.

This slide is a table — Course Agenda. The slide title is: Course Agenda. The slide says: Total: 8 modules · ~18 hours. The table header columns are: Day, Theme, Modules, Duration. Table row: **1**, Foundations, 1–3 Intro, install, modeling, ~6 h. Table row: **2**, Working with data, 4–5 Query language, aggregation, ~6 h. Table row: **3**, Performance and production, 6–8 Indexes, scale, practices, ~6 h.

The slide title is: Introduction to NoSQL Databases. The slide says: MongoDB is one member of a broader family of non-relational database technologies.

This slide lists key points under Module Learning Objectives. The slide title is: Module Learning Objectives. The slide says: By the end of this module you will be able to:. Bullet 1 on the slide: Define NoSQL as a category, not one product. Bullet 2 on the slide: Compare document, key-value, column-family, and graph models. Bullet 3 on the slide: Explain MongoDB documents, collections, and BSON. Bullet 4 on the slide: Describe the basic MongoDB architecture. Bullet 5 on the slide: Select workloads that are — and are not — good MongoDB candidates.

This slide includes a diagram — The Changing Application Data Landscape. The slide title is: The Changing Application Data Landscape. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Key message: Modern data is often hierarchical, varied, and continuously changing. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Rapidly changing requirements. Bullet 2 on the slide: Large and diverse datasets. Bullet 3 on the slide: JSON-based APIs. Bullet 4 on the slide: Cloud-native, distributed apps. Bullet 5 on the slide: High-volume user activity. Bullet 6 on the slide: Global availability. The figure on this slide is titled: Structured data evolving into hierarchical, rapidly changing application data.

This slide includes a diagram — Structured vs Semi-Structured vs Unstructured. The slide title is: Structured vs Semi-Structured vs Unstructured. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: MongoDB is strongest on semi-structured, hierarchical application data. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Structured: rows and columns with a declared schema. Bullet 2 on the slide: Semi-structured: nested JSON-like records; fields can vary. Bullet 3 on the slide: Unstructured: images, logs, and media with no field layout. The figure on this slide is titled: Side-by-side structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data.

This slide includes a diagram — Where Relational Databases Work Well. The slide title is: Where Relational Databases Work Well. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Key message: NoSQL is not a universal replacement for relational databases. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Structured, predictable schemas. Bullet 2 on the slide: Strong relationships between tables. Bullet 3 on the slide: Complex multi-table transactions. Bullet 4 on the slide: Mature SQL reporting. Bullet 5 on the slide: Financial and accounting systems. The figure on this slide is titled: Application connected to normalized tables with keys and relationships.

This slide includes a diagram — Challenges with Traditional Relational Models. The slide title is: Challenges with Traditional Relational Models. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Example: customers · addresses · orders · order_items · payments. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Rigid schemas and frequent migrations. Bullet 2 on the slide: Complex joins to rebuild one object. Bullet 3 on the slide: Object-relational mapping overhead. Bullet 4 on the slide: Horizontal scaling is harder than one server. Bullet 5 on the slide: Many tables for one business object. The figure on this slide is titled: One order reconstructed by joining many tables.

This slide includes a diagram — What Does NoSQL Mean?. The slide title is: What Does NoSQL Mean?. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: NoSQL commonly means “Not Only SQL.”. The slide says: Key message: NoSQL is a category, not one standard technology. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Flexible or non-tabular models. Bullet 2 on the slide: Horizontal scaling and availability. Bullet 3 on the slide: Application-oriented schemas. The figure on this slide is titled: SQL versus NoSQL comparison of schema, storage, relationships, scaling.

This slide includes a diagram — Why Organizations Adopt NoSQL. The slide title is: Why Organizations Adopt NoSQL. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Business drivers. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Faster delivery of new features. Bullet 2 on the slide: Unpredictable data shapes. Bullet 3 on the slide: Global user growth. Bullet 4 on the slide: Cloud deployment. Bullet 5 on the slide: High throughput and availability. The figure on this slide is titled: Application growth leading to flexibility, scale, availability, and faster delivery.

This slide includes a diagram — The Four Major NoSQL Database Types. The slide title is: The Four Major NoSQL Database Types. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. The table header columns are: Type, Primary structure. In the table, Document: JSON-like documents. In the table, Key-value: Key mapped to a value. In the table, Column-family: Rows with flexible columns. In the table, Graph: Nodes and relationships. The figure on this slide is titled: Four NoSQL branches: document, key-value, column-family, graph.

This slide includes a diagram — Document Databases. The slide title is: Document Databases. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Examples: MongoDB, Couchbase. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Database → collection → document. Bullet 2 on the slide: Fields, nested objects, arrays. Bullet 3 on the slide: Natural application objects. Bullet 4 on the slide: Flexible fields; fewer joins for many reads. The figure on this slide is titled: Collection of JSON-like documents with fields, arrays, and nested objects.

This slide includes a diagram — Key-Value Databases. The slide title is: Key-Value Databases. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Structure: Key → Value. The slide says: Example: Redis. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Sessions, caching, carts. Bullet 2 on the slide: Fast lookup by a known key. Bullet 3 on the slide: Querying inside the value may be limited. The figure on this slide is titled: Session and cart keys mapped directly to values.

This slide includes a diagram — Column-Family Databases. The slide title is: Column-Family Databases. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Use cases: telemetry, events, time-series ingest. The slide says: Examples: Cassandra, HBase. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Rows with flexible columns. Bullet 2 on the slide: Grouped into column families. Bullet 3 on the slide: Built for large distributed writes. The figure on this slide is titled: Flexible rows organized into column families.

This slide includes a diagram — Graph Databases. The slide title is: Graph Databases. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Use cases: fraud, social, recommendations. The slide says: Example: Neo4j. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Nodes = entities. Bullet 2 on the slide: Edges = relationships. Bullet 3 on the slide: Properties describe both. The figure on this slide is titled: Customers, products, and purchases as nodes and relationships.

This slide includes a diagram — Choosing the Right Database Model. The slide title is: Choosing the Right Database Model. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Begin with access patterns, consistency, relationships, and scale. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. The table header columns are: Scenario, Model. In the table, Session lookup: Key-value. In the table, Product catalog: Document. In the table, Social graph: Graph. In the table, Telemetry ingest: Column-family. In the table, Financial ledger: Relational. The figure on this slide is titled: Four-way comparison of structure, access pattern, and use case.

This slide includes a diagram — Database Selection Decision Flow. The slide title is: Database Selection Decision Flow. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Ask, in order:. The slide says: 1. Are paths the query?. The slide says: 2. Is it a direct key lookup?. The slide says: 3. Are attributes varied and nested?. The slide says: 4. Are multi-table transactions mandatory?. The slide says: 5. Is the load massive distributed writes?. The slide says: Then pick a product inside that model. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Number 1 on the slide: Are paths the query?. Number 2 on the slide: Is it a direct key lookup?. Number 3 on the slide: Are attributes varied and nested?. Number 4 on the slide: Are multi-table transactions mandatory?. Number 5 on the slide: Is the load massive distributed writes?. The figure on this slide is titled: Decision flow from workload need to database model.

This slide includes a diagram — `mongod` vs. `mongosh`. The slide title is: `mongod` vs. `mongosh`. You will also see the heading: mongod vs. mongosh. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: mongod accepts connections, processes operations, manages files and indexes, writes logs, and enforces configured security. The slide says: mongosh sends commands and prints results. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. The figure on this slide is titled: Side-by-side mongod server responsibilities versus mongosh client. The code on the slide reads: mongod = server mongosh = client.

This slide includes a diagram — Three Clients, One Deployment. The slide title is: Three Clients, One Deployment. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: Shell, Compass, and an application driver all target the same MongoDB. The slide says: They are different interfaces, not different databases. The slide says: Drivers show up again in Module 8. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. The figure on this slide is titled: mongosh, Compass, and driver converging on one deployment.

This slide includes a diagram — MongoDB Configuration File. The slide title is: MongoDB Configuration File. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. Bullet 6 on the slide: Process management. The figure on this slide is titled: Config file branching into storage, logging, network, security, replication, process.

The slide says: Data directory: collections, indexes, storage-engine files, metadata. The slide says: Log directory: startup, connections, warnings, authentication failures, config errors, shutdown. This slide includes a diagram — Common Connection Problems. The slide title is: Common Connection Problems. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. This slide includes a diagram — Relational Modeling vs Document Modeling. The slide title is: Relational Modeling vs Document Modeling. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The figure on this slide is titled: Relational approach compared with document approach.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Keep products and customers as collections. Bullet 3 on the slide: Reviews stay independent. The figure on this slide is titled: Relational tables transformed into MongoDB collections.

This slide includes a diagram — Join-Based Retrieval vs Document Retrieval. The slide title is: Join-Based Retrieval vs Document Retrieval. The slide says: <div class="cols">. This slide includes a diagram — Relationship Types. The slide title is: Relationship Types. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. Bullet 3 on the slide: Size, growth, ownership, and access direction decide the shape. The figure on this slide is titled: Cardinality spectrum from 1:1 to many-to-many.

Bullet 2 on the slide: Reference when the child has its own lifecycle. The figure on this slide is titled: Embedded contact versus referenced profile.

This slide includes a diagram — One-to-Few Relationships. The slide title is: One-to-Few Relationships. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. This slide includes a diagram — One-to-Many Relationships. The slide title is: One-to-Many Relationships. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. Bullet 2 on the slide: One or few and bounded → embed. Bullet 3 on the slide: Many or unbounded → reference. The figure on this slide is titled: Cardinality leading to embed or reference.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Risks: duplication, growth, bulk updates. The figure on this slide is titled: Advantages and risks of embedding.

This slide includes a diagram — Referencing Related Data. The slide title is: Referencing Related Data. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. Bullet 3 on the slide: Use the table; do not memorize slogans only. The figure on this slide is titled: Considerations for embed versus reference.

This slide includes a diagram — Common MongoDB Schema Patterns. The slide title is: Common MongoDB Schema Patterns. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Reusable approaches, not mandatory templates. Bullet 2 on the slide: Attribute, Bucket, Subset, Extended reference. Bullet 3 on the slide: Computed, Outlier, Polymorphic. The figure on this slide is titled: Seven named MongoDB schema patterns.

This slide includes a diagram — Attribute Pattern. The slide title is: Attribute Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Many similar optional attributes. Bullet 2 on the slide: attributes: [ { name, value } ]. Bullet 3 on the slide: Easier to index than fifty sparse fields. The figure on this slide is titled: Named fields versus name-value attribute array.

This slide includes a diagram — Bucket Pattern. The slide title is: Bucket Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Group measurements into a bounded document. Bullet 2 on the slide: Sensor hour, metrics, events. Bullet 3 on the slide: Fewer documents, controlled growth. The figure on this slide is titled: Hour bucket containing a bounded readings array.

This slide includes a diagram — Subset Pattern. The slide title is: Subset Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Keep the hot subset on the parent. Bullet 2 on the slide: Full set lives elsewhere. Bullet 3 on the slide: Example: three recent reviews plus average rating. The figure on this slide is titled: Product subset versus full reviews collection.

This slide includes a diagram — Extended Reference Pattern. The slide title is: Extended Reference Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Copy frequently displayed fields onto the reference. Bullet 2 on the slide: Order stores customer name and tier. Bullet 3 on the slide: Tradeoff: those copies may need sync. The figure on this slide is titled: Order carrying a small customer summary.

This slide includes a diagram — Computed Pattern. The slide title is: Computed Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Store the result instead of recomputing on every read. Bullet 2 on the slide: Average rating, order total, lifetime value. Bullet 3 on the slide: Must update when the source changes. The figure on this slide is titled: Stored rating summary on a product.

This slide includes a diagram — Outlier Pattern. The slide title is: Outlier Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Most documents follow the normal design. Bullet 2 on the slide: Rare extremes get a different store. Bullet 3 on the slide: Do not distort the schema for one viral product. The figure on this slide is titled: Typical products versus viral products.

This slide includes a diagram — Polymorphic Pattern. The slide title is: Polymorphic Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Different types share one collection and a core. Bullet 2 on the slide: A type or category field distinguishes them. Bullet 3 on the slide: Same workflows, varied attributes. The figure on this slide is titled: BOOK and LAPTOP documents in one collection.

This slide includes a diagram — Choosing an Appropriate Pattern. The slide title is: Choosing an Appropriate Pattern. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Start from the requirement, then pick a pattern. Bullet 2 on the slide: You may combine patterns in one model. The figure on this slide is titled: Requirements mapped to schema patterns.

This slide includes a diagram — Combining Schema Patterns. The slide title is: Combining Schema Patterns. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Patterns compose on one document. Bullet 2 on the slide: Catalog: polymorphic + attribute + computed + subset. The slide title is: `$set`, `$unset`, Numeric Operators, `$rename`. You will also see the heading: $set, $unset, Numeric Operators, $rename. The slide says: Use consistent numeric types. Prefer $inc on integers. Be careful multiplying money. The code on the slide reads: { $set: { featured: true, "attributes.warrantyYears": 2 } } { $unset: { temporaryNote: "" } } { $inc: { stockQuantity: 5 } } { $mul: { price: 1.05 } } // beware Decimal128 vs double { $min: { lowestPrice: Decimal128("45.00") } } { $rename: { productName: "name" } }.

This slide includes a diagram — Replace vs `$set` vs Upsert. The slide title is: Replace vs `$set` vs Upsert. You will also see the heading: Replace vs $set vs Upsert. This slide includes a diagram — Partial Indexes. The slide title is: Partial Indexes. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Index only documents matching a filter. Bullet 2 on the slide: Example: partialFilterExpression: { active: true }. Bullet 3 on the slide: Smaller index, lower maintenance. Bullet 4 on the slide: Queries generally need to be compatible with the filter. The figure on this slide is titled: Partial versus sparse selection rules.

The slide title is: Sparse Indexes. The slide says: A sparse index omits documents that do not contain the indexed field. The slide says: Less flexible than a partial index: the rule is only “field exists,” not an arbitrary filter. The code on the slide reads: db.products.createIndex( { discountCode: 1 }, { sparse: true } ).

This slide is a table — Partial vs. Sparse Indexes. The slide title is: Partial vs. Sparse Indexes. The slide says: Preference: partial when you can state the subset clearly. The table header columns are: Consideration, Partial, Sparse. In the table, Selection rule — Explicit filter. Use case on slide: Indexed field exists. In the table, Flexibility — Higher. Use case on slide: Lower. In the table, Common use — Active / status subset. Use case on slide: Optional field. In the table, Query compatibility — Must align with filter. Use case on slide: Respect missing fields.

This slide includes a diagram — Text, Wildcard, Geospatial, and Hashed. The slide title is: Text, Wildcard, Geospatial, and Hashed. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Text: $text word search — one text index per collection. Bullet 2 on the slide: Wildcard: attributes.$** for dynamic paths. Bullet 3 on the slide: Geospatial: 2dsphere on GeoJSON points. Bullet 4 on the slide: Hashed: equality distribution; no ordered range. Bullet 5 on the slide: Advanced search often belongs in a dedicated search product. The figure on this slide is titled: Specialized index types.

The slide title is: Text and Wildcard Examples. The slide says: training_store product attributes vary by category (laptop vs shoe vs book). Wildcard can index those paths; it is still a write and storage cost. The code on the slide reads: db.products.createIndex({ name: "text", description: "text" }) db.products.find({ $text: { $search: "wireless keyboard" } }) db.products.createIndex({ "attributes.$**": 1 }).

The slide title is: Geospatial and Hashed Examples. The slide says: Use for nearby stores, delivery zones, asset locations. The slide says: Hashed keys support hashed sharding and equality distribution. They do not preserve sort order or range scans. The code on the slide reads: db.stores.createIndex({ location: "2dsphere" }). The code on the slide reads: db.events.createIndex({ tenantId: "hashed" }).

This slide includes a diagram — Choosing the Appropriate Index Type. The slide title is: Choosing the Appropriate Index Type. The slide says: <div class="cols">. Bullet 2 on the slide: Filter and sort on several fields → compound. Bullet 3 on the slide: Unique identifier → unique. Bullet 4 on the slide: Array elements → multikey. Bullet 5 on the slide: Active subset → partial. Bullet 6 on the slide: Expire rows → TTL. Bullet 7 on the slide: Dynamic attributes → wildcard (with caution). The figure on this slide is titled: Requirement to index-type mapping.

The slide title is: Lab 6.7 — Steps 3–4. The slide says: Follow along (Windows) — key steps:. Step 3 — Create sessions and TTL. Step 4 — Observe asynchronous expiration. Bullet 1 on the slide: Do: Run: ```javascript db.sessions.drop() db.sessions.insertMany([ { sessionId: "S1", user: "aisha", expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 60 60 1000) }, { sessionId: "S-EXPIRED", user: "temp", expiresAt: new Date(Date.now(). Bullet 2 on the slide: Expected: ttl_sessions_expires_at exists with expireAfterSeconds: 0. Two documents are present immediately after insert. Bullet 3 on the slide: Do: Wait about 60 seconds (TTL monitor interval), then db.sessions.find(). Do not block the class if the expired row is still there — record that expiration is asynchronous. Bullet 4 on the slide: Expected: S-EXPIRED may disappear after the TTL thread runs. The lab succeeds if the index is configured correctly even if the delete has not fired yet. Never treat TTL a.

Let's look at Common Write-Concern Levels. The slide title is: Common Write-Concern Levels. The slide says: Primary acknowledgment (w: 1). Bullet 2 on the slide: Heavy write volume or large operations. Bullet 3 on the slide: Index differences and resource contention. Bullet 4 on the slide: Maintenance and secondary-specific workloads. This slide includes a diagram — What Is Sharding?. The slide title is: What Is Sharding?. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Partitions a collection across multiple shards. Bullet 2 on the slide: Each shard stores only part of the sharded dataset. Bullet 3 on the slide: Supports storage, query, and write scale. Bullet 4 on the slide: Adds significant operational complexity. The figure on this slide is titled: Three shards holding ranges.

This slide lists key points under Why Applications Need Sharding. The slide title is: Why Applications Need Sharding. The slide says: Consider sharding when:. The slide says: Warning: shard to a measured need, not a slide from a conference. Bullet 1 on the slide: Dataset exceeds one replica set’s practical capacity. Bullet 2 on the slide: Read or write demand exceeds one replica set. Bullet 3 on the slide: Working set no longer fits effectively. Bullet 4 on the slide: Geographic placement is required. Bullet 5 on the slide: Vertical scaling is no longer sustainable.

Bullet 16 on the slide: Expected: Usually a different design: pre-aggregated reports, an analytics replica/cluster, or accepting scatter-gather for a rare job — not a shard key that hurts the OL.

This slide includes a diagram — Hot Shards and Hotspots. The slide title is: Hot Shards and Hotspots. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: One shard takes disproportionate writes, reads, growth, CPU, or network. Bullet 2 on the slide: Causes: monotonic keys, dominant tenants, skew, bad routing, zones, recent-data concentration. The figure on this slide is titled: One hot shard.

This slide includes a diagram — Distributed Writes. The slide title is: Distributed Writes. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Client → mongos → destination shard primary. Bullet 2 on the slide: That replica set replicates the oplog. Bullet 3 on the slide: Ack follows write concern. Bullet 4 on the slide: Sharding and replication share the write path. The figure on this slide is titled: Write path through mongos and shard RS.

Let's look at Unique Constraints in Sharded Collections. The slide title is: Unique Constraints in Sharded Collections. The slide says: Unique indexes on sharded collections need the uniqueness pattern to be compatible with the shard key. The slide says: Design business identifiers together with the shard key when global uniqueness is required. The slide says: Confirm version- and deployment-specific rules before a production unique index. Do not assume orderNumber unique works the same as on a replica set.

This slide lists key points under Transactions in Sharded Clusters. The slide title is: Transactions in Sharded Clusters. The slide says: Multi-document transactions can span shards. Cost:. The slide says: Good modeling and shard keys reduce unnecessary cross-shard transactions. Prefer single-document or single-shard updates when the domain allows. Bullet 1 on the slide: Extra network and coordination. Bullet 2 on the slide: Higher latency and failure complexity. Bullet 3 on the slide: More resource use.

Let's look at Resharding Concepts. The slide title is: Resharding Concepts. The slide says: Workloads evolve. A key that once distributed well may hotspot or scatter later. The slide says: Resharding changes distribution to a new key. It is a major operational activity: capacity, compatibility, monitoring, performance tests, failure and rollback planning. The slide says: Choosing carefully the first time is cheaper than resharding under pressure.

The slide title is: Sharded-Cluster Status. The slide says: Useful views: shards, sharded DBs/collections, keys, distribution, balancer, zones. The slide says: Availability depends on privileges and whether you are actually on mongos. The code on the slide reads: sh.status().

This slide lists key points under Sharding Operational Practices. The slide title is: Sharding Operational Practices. Bullet 1 on the slide: Choose keys from measured workload. Bullet 2 on the slide: Replica sets for shards; redundant mongos. Bullet 3 on the slide: Protect config servers. Bullet 4 on the slide: Monitor routing, distribution, balancer. Bullet 5 on the slide: Test shard failure. Bullet 6 on the slide: Avoid uncontrolled scatter-gather on the hot path. Bullet 7 on the slide: Back up the distributed deployment.

Let's look at Sharded-Cluster Failure Scenarios. The slide title is: Sharded-Cluster Failure Scenarios. The slide says: One shard member fails — the shard replica set may stay available if it keeps a primary. The slide says: Shard loses primary — operations that need that shard wait on election. The slide says: One mongos fails — clients use another router if configured. The slide says: Config-server problems — metadata and management suffer; this is serious.

This slide lists key points under Query Design Best Practices. The slide title is: Query Design Best Practices. Bullet 1 on the slide: Use selective filters and correct BSON types. Bullet 2 on the slide: Prefer indexed fields for recurring shapes. Bullet 3 on the slide: Return only required documents and fields. Bullet 4 on the slide: Sort deterministically; limit and paginate. Bullet 5 on the slide: Avoid uncontrolled regular expressions. Bullet 6 on the slide: Inspect important query plans.

This slide includes a diagram — Retrieve Only Required Documents. The slide title is: Retrieve Only Required Documents. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The figure on this slide is titled: Selective filter versus collection scan.

This slide includes a diagram — Return Only Required Fields. The slide title is: Return Only Required Fields. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The figure on this slide is titled: Projection shrinks the payload.

This slide includes a diagram — Use Appropriate BSON Types. The slide title is: Use Appropriate BSON Types. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Timestamps → Date. Bullet 2 on the slide: Exact money → Decimal128. Bullet 3 on the slide: Flags → Boolean. Bullet 4 on the slide: Quantities → integer types. Bullet 5 on the slide: Ids → ObjectId or a consistent business id. Bullet 6 on the slide: Wrong types break filters, sorts, math, and indexes. This slide includes a diagram — Avoid Expensive Query Patterns. The slide title is: Avoid Expensive Query Patterns. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Leading-wildcard or unanchored regex. Bullet 2 on the slide: Large skip-based pagination. Bullet 3 on the slide: Broad negative filters. Bullet 4 on the slide: Missing shard-key predicates. Bullet 5 on the slide: Huge result sets and app-side joins. Bullet 6 on the slide: Sorts without a supporting index. Bullet 7 on the slide: Examining far more documents than you return. The figure on this slide is titled: Expensive query pattern grid.

This slide lists key points under Aggregation Pipeline Best Practices. The slide title is: Aggregation Pipeline Best Practices. Bullet 1 on the slide: Start from the correct collection. Bullet 2 on the slide: Filter early when the logic allows. Bullet 3 on the slide: Build one stage at a time and inspect output. Bullet 4 on the slide: Control array expansion. Bullet 5 on the slide: Avoid unnecessary $lookup. Bullet 6 on the slide: Handle null and missing values. Bullet 7 on the slide: Validate calculations on a tiny sample. Bullet 8 on the slide: Shape the final output; review the plan.

This slide includes a diagram — Reduce Pipeline Input Early. The slide title is: Reduce Pipeline Input Early. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Large collection → selective $match → smaller working set → expensive stages. Bullet 2 on the slide: $match after $group filters grouped results — different job. Bullet 3 on the slide: Early filters reduce work in $unwind, $lookup, and $group. The figure on this slide is titled: Filter before expensive stages.

This slide includes a diagram — Control `$unwind` Expansion. The slide title is: Control `$unwind` Expansion. You will also see the heading: Control $unwind Expansion. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: 100,000 orders × 10 items → 1,000,000 documents. Bullet 2 on the slide: Before unwind: filter, drop unused fields, confirm the array is required. Bullet 3 on the slide: Estimate the expansion factor. Bullet 4 on the slide: Do not sum parent totals after unwind. The figure on this slide is titled: Unwind multiplies document count.

This slide includes a diagram — Use `$lookup` Deliberately. The slide title is: Use `$lookup` Deliberately. You will also see the heading: Use $lookup Deliberately. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Is the data already embedded on purpose?. Bullet 2 on the slide: Is the join required for this request?. Bullet 3 on the slide: Is the foreign field indexed?. Bullet 4 on the slide: How many matches? Will it create a large array?. Bullet 5 on the slide: Can the foreign pipeline filter and project?. Bullet 6 on the slide: Hot path versus occasional report?. The figure on this slide is titled: Questions before adding lookup.

This slide includes a diagram — Demo 8.3 — Tune an Aggregation Pipeline. The slide title is: Demo 8.3 — Tune an Aggregation Pipeline. The slide says: <div class="cols">. This slide includes a diagram — Exercise 8.4 — Optimize an Aggregation Pipeline. The slide title is: Exercise 8.4 — Optimize an Aggregation Pipeline. The slide says: <div class="cols">. This slide lists key points under Indexing Best Practices. The slide title is: Indexing Best Practices. Bullet 1 on the slide: Index recurring query shapes. Bullet 2 on the slide: Use compound indexes deliberately. Bullet 3 on the slide: Start from Equality–Sort–Range. Bullet 4 on the slide: Review prefixes; measure with explain(). Bullet 5 on the slide: Hide before you drop; monitor usage. Bullet 6 on the slide: Account for write and storage cost. Bullet 7 on the slide: Revisit indexes as the workload changes.

This slide includes a diagram — MongoDB Security Principles. The slide title is: MongoDB Security Principles. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Identity, authentication, authorization. Bullet 2 on the slide: Network isolation, encryption, secret protection. Bullet 3 on the slide: Auditing, patching, backups, monitoring. Bullet 4 on the slide: No single control is enough. The figure on this slide is titled: Layered MongoDB security controls.

Let's look at Authentication. The slide title is: Authentication. The slide says: Authentication verifies identity. The slide says: Sources may include database users, certificates, enterprise identity, cloud identity, and workload identities. The slide says: Avoid shared admin accounts, default or weak passwords, anonymous access, and long-lived secrets without rotation.

This slide lists key points under Authorization and Role-Based Access. The slide title is: Authorization and Role-Based Access. The slide says: Authorization decides permitted operations:. The slide says: Roles should match responsibilities — not job titles copied from email. Bullet 1 on the slide: Read or read/write application data. Bullet 2 on the slide: Manage indexes. Bullet 3 on the slide: Inspect monitoring. Bullet 4 on the slide: Administer users and backups. Bullet 5 on the slide: Administer the cluster.

This slide includes a diagram — Principle of Least Privilege. The slide title is: Principle of Least Privilege. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Grant only what the workload needs. Bullet 2 on the slide: App: readWrite on its database. Bullet 3 on the slide: Reporting: read on approved collections. Bullet 4 on the slide: Backup and monitoring: their own roles. Bullet 5 on the slide: Never put clusterAdmin in application code. The figure on this slide is titled: Least-privilege identity ceiling.

This slide includes a diagram — Network Security. The slide title is: Network Security. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Private networks, firewalls, allowlists. Bullet 2 on the slide: Segmentation and controlled admin paths. Bullet 3 on the slide: No unnecessary public exposure. Bullet 4 on the slide: Separate application and management access. Bullet 5 on the slide: Review rules continuously. The figure on this slide is titled: Private network then allowlist.

This slide includes a diagram — Encryption in Transit and at Rest. The slide title is: Encryption in Transit and at Rest. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Transit (TLS): app, admins, replica members, shard components, backup paths. Bullet 2 on the slide: Validate certificates — encryption without identity checks is weak. Bullet 3 on the slide: At rest: disks, snapshots, backups, temp files, exports, logs. Bullet 4 on the slide: Pair with key management and access policy. The figure on this slide is titled: TLS in transit and encryption at rest.

This slide includes a diagram — Application Credential Management. The slide title is: Application Credential Management. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Do not store secrets in source, images, screenshots, shared docs, or open config files. Bullet 2 on the slide: Use a secret manager, protected injection, workload identity. Bullet 3 on the slide: Rotate, separate environments, audit access. The figure on this slide is titled: Secrets stay out of source control.

Let's look at Data Classification and Sensitive Fields. The slide title is: Data Classification and Sensitive Fields. The slide says: Classify PII, payment data, tokens, health, financial, and confidential business fields. The slide says: Then define who may access them, where they live, how long they stay, masking, field-level protection, and audit. The slide says: Do not put password hashes on orders. Do not copy production dumps to intern laptops.

Let's look at Auditing and Security Logging. The slide title is: Auditing and Security Logging. The slide says: Log authentication success/failure, user and role changes, admin and config operations, collection changes, sensitive access, backup and restore. The slide says: Protect logs from tampering and from leaking the secrets they might contain.

This slide lists key points under Secure Configuration Practices. The slide title is: Secure Configuration Practices. Bullet 1 on the slide: Enable authentication; restrict bindings; encrypt connections. Bullet 2 on the slide: Least-privilege roles; disable unnecessary exposure. Bullet 3 on the slide: Rotate secrets; separate dev, test, and production. Bullet 4 on the slide: Patch; protect backups; review config changes. Bullet 5 on the slide: Keep an asset and owner inventory.

This slide includes a diagram — Security Anti-Patterns. The slide title is: Security Anti-Patterns. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Public database port; authentication off. Bullet 2 on the slide: Shared administrator credentials. Bullet 3 on the slide: Secrets in source control; no TLS. Bullet 4 on the slide: App running as cluster admin. Bullet 5 on the slide: Dev accounts in production. Bullet 6 on the slide: Unprotected backups; secrets in logs. Bullet 7 on the slide: No monitoring or access review. The figure on this slide is titled: Security anti-pattern grid.

Let's look at Backup and Recovery Fundamentals. The slide title is: Backup and Recovery Fundamentals. The slide says: A strategy must define what, how often, where, protection, retention, restore steps, owner, and test cadence. The slide says: A backup is valuable only if it can be restored.

This slide includes a diagram — Replication vs. Backup. The slide title is: Replication vs. Backup. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Replication helps with server and some infrastructure failure and planned maintenance. Bullet 2 on the slide: It does not independently protect against drops, malice, bad migrations, or slow corruption. Bullet 3 on the slide: Mistakes replicate to every member. The figure on this slide is titled: Replica sets versus backups.

This slide lists key points under Backup Strategy. The slide title is: Backup Strategy. The slide says: Combine as the platform allows:. Bullet 1 on the slide: Scheduled snapshots and/or continuous backup. Bullet 2 on the slide: Point-in-time recovery. Bullet 3 on the slide: Logical exports for subsets or migration. Bullet 4 on the slide: Offsite or separate-account storage. Bullet 5 on the slide: Retention, encryption, restore testing, named owners.

This slide is a table — Logical vs. Physical Backup. The slide title is: Logical vs. Physical Backup. The slide says: Choose from scale, RPO/RTO, and platform — not from habit. The table header columns are: Logical, Physical. In the table, Exports database content: Copies files or snapshots. In the table, Portable subsets: Efficient full recovery. In the table, Slower at large scale: Needs compatible restore. In the table, Migration and selected data: Large deployments.

This slide includes a diagram — Recovery Point and Recovery Time Objectives. The slide title is: Recovery Point and Recovery Time Objectives. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: RPO: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (example: 15 minutes). Bullet 2 on the slide: RTO: maximum acceptable time to restore service (example: 2 hours). Bullet 3 on the slide: Backup frequency and restore design must beat those numbers. The figure on this slide is titled: RPO versus RTO.

This slide includes a diagram — Restore Testing. The slide title is: Restore Testing. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Readable backup, credentials and keys, procedure, duration. Bullet 2 on the slide: Data consistency, app connectivity, indexes, users/roles. Bullet 3 on the slide: Documentation that someone else can follow. Bullet 4 on the slide: Successful backup jobs do not prove recovery. The figure on this slide is titled: Restore test goes beyond a green job.

Let's look at Point-in-Time Recovery and Disaster Recovery. The slide title is: Point-in-Time Recovery and Disaster Recovery. The slide says: PITR restores to a moment before a bad drop, deploy, bulk update, or app corruption — if the platform kept history. The slide says: A DR plan names scenarios, architecture, backup location, region strategy, RPO/RTO, people, comms, app reconnect, validation, test schedule, and return-to-normal.

This slide includes a diagram — Monitoring Fundamentals. The slide title is: Monitoring Fundamentals. The slide says: <div class="cols">. The slide says: <div class="col-text">. The slide says: </div>. The slide says: <div class="col-visual">. Bullet 1 on the slide: Is it up? Is it fast enough?. Bullet 2 on the slide: Is workload or capacity changing?. Bullet 6 on the slide: Are users seeing errors?. The figure on this slide is titled: Questions a dashboard must answer.

Let's look at Database, Query, and Resource Metrics. The slide title is: Database, Query, and Resource Metrics. The slide says: Health: availability, op rates, latency, queues, connections, cache/working set, errors, data and index size. The slide says: Queries: slow ops, latency percentiles, examined vs returned, COLLSCAN, in-memory sorts, timeouts, heavy aggregations. The slide says: Resources: CPU, memory, disk capacity/latency/throughput, network, filesystem, container limits. The slide says: Symptoms often start in infrastructure, not in BSON.

Let's look at Replication, Sharding, and Connection Metrics. The slide title is: Replication, Sharding, and Connection Metrics. The slide says: Replication: primary, member health, lag, oplog window, elections, rollbacks, errors, secondary resource use. The slide says: Sharding: distribution, hot shards, mongos/CSRS health, balancer, migrations, targeted vs scatter-gather, zone compliance. The slide says: Connections: current, spawn rate, pool use, rejected, auth failures, leaks, sudden load. The slide says: Application pools must be sized on purpose.

Let's look at Logging Best Practices. The slide title is: Logging Best Practices. The slide says: Logs should be centralized, time-synced, searchable, access-controlled, retained, tamper-resistant, correlated with app and infra, and free of unnecessary secrets. The slide says: Useful fields: timestamp, component, host, severity, operation, error code, correlation id.

Bullet 3 on the slide: Linked to a runbook; tested periodically. Bullet 4 on the slide: Avoid alerts that only name a metric. The figure on this slide is titled: Quality of a good alert.

Let's look at Authentication and Authorization Troubleshooting. The slide title is: Authentication and Authorization Troubleshooting. The slide says: Authentication failure: username, password, auth source, certificate, expiry, URI encoding. The slide says: Authorization failure: roles, target database, operation, collection privileges, inheritance, recent grants/revokes. The slide says: A ping can succeed while inserts fail — that is authorization, not ‘Mongo is down’.

Let's look at Query, Aggregation, and Index Troubleshooting. The slide title is: Query, Aggregation, and Index Troubleshooting. The slide says: Query: db/collection, case, nested paths, BSON types, filter logic, arrays, projection, sort, indexes, explain, result size. The slide says: Aggregation: shape, stage order, field paths, per-stage output, group keys, nulls, types, unwind multiplication, lookup types, double count, time zones. The slide says: Index not used: leading fields, predicates, sort direction, types, partial filter, collation, selectivity, multikey, projection, competing indexes, actual stats.

Let's look at Replication, Sharding, and Capacity Troubleshooting. The slide title is: Replication, Sharding, and Capacity Troubleshooting. The slide says: Replication: primary, majority, member health, network, lag, oplog window, disk/CPU, elections, write concern, recent config. The slide says: Sharding: mongos, CSRS, shard health, shard-key predicates, targeting, hot shards, balancer, zones, migrations, cross-shard ops. The slide says: Capacity: latency, queues, disk, memory, CPU, connections, storage. Cause may be growth, bad queries, missing or extra indexes, huge documents, infra limits, or maintenance.

We are starting Exercise 8.14 — Production-Readiness Review for training_store. We have about 45 min for this lab. Produce a six-part action plan and an evidence-based production-readiness classification. The full lab guide is in slide-exercises/module-08/exercise-8.14-practical-challenge.md if you need extra detail. On Windows: PowerShell in the integrated terminal — Ctrl+backtick — and the Agent panel — Ctrl+I. Open the repo folder with File → Open Folder. Step 1 — Write model and performance recommendations. Step 2 — Write security, reliability, and monitoring. I'll give you a few minutes to work — raise your hand if you get stuck. The slide title is: Exercise 8.14 — Steps 1–2. The slide says: Lab guide: [Exercise 8.14](../slide-exercises/module-08/exercise-8.14-practical-challenge.md). The slide says: Follow along (Windows) — key steps:. Bullet 1 on the slide: Do: Correct BSON types; separate unbounded reviews; preserve order snapshots; add validation; plan migration. Then rewrite broad queries, add projections, tune the sales aggregation, recommend indexes, flag redundant indexes. Bullet 2 on the slide: Expected: A two-section note exists. Reviews are a collection. Prices are Decimal128. Queries are selective. Indexes follow ESR. At least one overlapping index is flagged. Bullet 3 on the slide: Do: Restrict network access; replace shared credentials; least privilege; TLS; secret storage; audit privileged activity. Test failover; review lag and oplog; define RPO/RTO; test restore. Add query, connection, storage, rep. Bullet 4 on the slide: Expected: Security list includes network, authn, authz, TLS, secrets. Reliability includes tested failover and restore plus RPO/RTO. Monitoring has owners, not only metri.

Now for Steps 3–3. Step 3 — Classify with evidence. I'll give you a few minutes to work — raise your hand if you get stuck. The slide title is: Exercise 8.14 — Steps 3–3. The slide says: Follow along (Windows) — key steps:. Bullet 1 on the slide: Do: Select Production-ready, Ready with conditions, or Not production-ready. Cite evidence from the current environment list (no validation, public network, untested restore, CPU-only monitoring, and the rest). Bullet 2 on the slide: Expected: Not production-ready is the defensible call. Ready with conditions is acceptable only if conditions are explicit and blocking. Production-ready is not justified.
